blocks.title: Indicator
blocks.text: An indicator is a substance that changes colour to mark a titration's end point. Acid-base indicators exhibit one colour in acid and another in base.

Most indicators used in acid-base titration are weak organic acids or weak organic bases. In solution a weak-acid indicator HIn can be represented by HIn gives H+ + In-, where In- is the anion part of the indicator. Because the reaction is reversible, both HIn and In- are present, and the colours displayed result from HIn and In- having different colours. In acidic solutions any In- ions present act as Bronsted bases and accept protons from the acid, so the indicator is present largely in the un-ionised form HIn. In basic solutions the OH- ions of the base combine with the H+ ions produced by the indicator, the indicator molecules ionise further to make up the loss of H+, and the indicator is present largely as its anion In-; the solution then shows the base-indicating colour, which for litmus is blue.

blocks.alt: A small blue H ball attached to a large grey In ball (HIn). An arrow to the right labelled In basic solution and an arrow to the left labelled In acidic solution lead to a blue H ball with a plus charge, plus a large red In ball with a minus charge.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.1: Unionized acid-base indicators and their ionised forms exist in an equilibrium (original drawing after the textbook's second Figure 9.1).

blocks.text: Different indicators change colour at different pH values; the colour depends on the relative amounts of HIn and In- at a given pH. Methyl red, for example, changes from red to yellow between pH 4.4 and 6.2: at pH 4.4 the indicator exists mostly as HIn molecules, which appear red. Figure 9.2 gives the ranges of some commonly used indicators.

blocks.alt: Two colour bars above a pH scale from 0 to 14. Methyl orange: red at low pH, changing through orange to yellow between about pH 3.2 and 4.5, yellow above. Phenolphthalein: colourless up to about pH 8.2, turning pink to red by about pH 10, red above.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.2: Range and color changes of some common Acid-Base indicators (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.2).
